s: Under reverse bias practically no current flows (only a tiny leakage current), so the junction behaves like an OFF (open) switch.
The depletion layer between two conducting regions also gives it a junction capacitance (used in varactor diodes).
mcqs.n: Some keys give A (capacitor) because a reverse-biased junction has capacitance; as a circuit element it acts as an OFF switch.

shortQuestions: (a) The base is made thin and lightly doped so that very few carriers coming from the emitter recombine in it. Almost all of them reach the collector, giving a small base current and a large current gain.

(b) The collector is made large because the collector–base junction is reverse biased at a higher voltage and most of the power (≈ I_CV_CE) is dissipated there; a large collector dissipates heat and collects the carriers efficiently.
The base is very thin and lightly doped, so only about 1–5% of the carriers injected from the emitter recombine with the few carriers in the base.
These recombinations form the small base current I_B; the remaining 95–99% are swept into the collector as I_C. So I_B ≪ I_C (I_C = βI_B).
Forward biasing the emitter–base junction lowers its barrier, so the emitter injects a large number of majority carriers into the base.
Reverse biasing the collector–base junction creates a strong field that sweeps the carriers reaching the base into the collector.
This bias (active region) is needed for normal transistor action and amplification.

NPN: the forward-biased emitter–base junction injects electrons from the N-type emitter into the thin P-type base. A few recombine with holes (base current); most diffuse across and are swept by the reverse-biased collector junction into the collector. I_E = I_B + I_C.
PNP: the same action occurs with holes as the majority carriers injected from the P-type emitter, and all bias polarities and current directions are reversed.
In both, a small base current controls a large collector current.
N-type: intrinsic Si/Ge doped with a pentavalent (donor) impurity such as P, As, Sb; electrons are majority carriers, holes minority; donor ions are positive.
P-type: doped with a trivalent (acceptor) impurity such as B, Al, Ga, In; holes are majority carriers, electrons minority; acceptor ions are negative.
The P-type material is made of neutral silicon atoms and neutral trivalent impurity atoms; doping adds no net charge.

Each hole created by an acceptor atom is balanced by the negative charge of that ionised acceptor. Total positive charge (holes) equals total negative charge (acceptor ions + electrons), so the crystal is electrically neutral.
The common-emitter amplifier gives a high current gain (β ≈ 50–300), a high voltage gain and the highest power gain of the three configurations.
Its input resistance is moderate and its output resistance moderately high, so stages can be cascaded easily. Hence CE is the most widely used amplifier configuration.
A small change in the input (base) current produces a large change in the output (collector) current: ΔI_C = β ΔI_B, with β typically 100 or more.
Thus the transistor amplifies current, and with a load resistor this also gives voltage and power amplification.
Each trivalent atom accepts an electron from a neighbouring Si bond and creates one hole: 10 trivalent atoms give 10 holes.
Thermal generation at 25 °C is negligible for so few atoms (intrinsic carriers ≈ 1.5 × 10¹⁰ per 5 × 10²² atoms, i.e. about 0.003 pairs for 10¹⁰ atoms).
So there are about 10 holes and practically no free electrons.
longQuestions: In a solid the energy levels of the atoms broaden into bands; the important ones are the valence band and the conduction band, separated by the forbidden energy gap E_g.
Insulator: the valence band is full, the conduction band empty, and E_g is large (> 3 eV, e.g. diamond ≈ 6 eV); electrons cannot be excited across it, so there is no conduction.

Semiconductor: E_g is small (Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.7 eV). At 0 K it is an insulator; at room temperature some electrons jump into the conduction band, leaving holes, so it conducts moderately; conductivity rises with temperature.
Conductor: the valence and conduction bands overlap (no gap) or the band is partly filled, so plenty of free electrons are available and conductivity is high.
When P and N regions are joined, electrons diffuse from N to P and holes from P to N, where they recombine.
This leaves a thin region near the junction with no free carriers but with uncovered ions: positive donor ions on the N side and negative acceptor ions on the P side — the depletion layer.
These ions set up an electric field and a potential barrier (≈ 0.7 V for Si, 0.3 V for Ge) that stops further diffusion; equilibrium is reached when diffusion and drift balance.
Energy band diagram: the bands on the P side are raised relative to the N side by eV₀; the Fermi level is the same throughout, and electrons need energy eV₀ to cross.

Significance: the depletion layer makes the junction conduct in one direction only — forward bias narrows it (conduction), reverse bias widens it (blocking). It also gives the junction its capacitance.
A half-wave rectifier converts a.c. into d.c. using one diode in series with a load resistor R_L across the secondary of a transformer.
During the positive half cycle the diode is forward biased; it conducts and current flows through R_L, giving an output voltage.
During the negative half cycle the diode is reverse biased; it does not conduct and the output is zero.
The output is a series of positive half-cycle pulses (pulsating d.c.) in one direction; a capacitor filter can smooth it.

An NPN transistor in common-emitter mode: the emitter–base junction is forward biased (V_BB) and the collector–base junction reverse biased (V_CC) through a load resistor R_C. The input signal is applied between base and emitter.
The signal changes the base current slightly by ΔI_B; this produces a large change in collector current ΔI_C = βΔI_B.
The output voltage V_CE = V_CC − I_CR_C therefore changes by ΔV_out = −βΔI_B R_C, much larger than the input change.
Voltage gain A_v = −β R_C/r_i; the negative sign means the output is 180° out of phase with the input. In this way a weak signal is amplified.
Half-wave rectifier: a.c. source (transformer secondary) → one diode in series → load resistor R_L. Output: positive half cycles only.

Full-wave (centre-tap) rectifier: transformer with centre-tapped secondary; two diodes D₁ and D₂ connected to the two ends, their outputs joined at one end of R_L, the other end of R_L to the centre tap. Each diode conducts on alternate half cycles, so current flows through R_L in the same direction during both halves.
Full-wave bridge rectifier: four diodes in a bridge; two conduct in each half cycle. (Circuit diagrams as in the textbook figures.)

Half-wave rectifier — advantages: simple, cheap, only one diode, no centre-tapped transformer. Disadvantages: uses only half of each cycle, low efficiency (≈ 40.6%), large ripple (ripple frequency = f), output more difficult to smooth.
Full-wave rectifier — advantages: uses both halves of the cycle, higher average output (2V₀/π) and efficiency (≈ 81.2%), smaller ripple at twice the supply frequency, easier to filter.

Disadvantages of full-wave: needs two diodes and a centre-tapped transformer (or four diodes in a bridge), so it is more costly; each diode must withstand a larger peak inverse voltage in the centre-tap type.
Definitions: α = I_C/I_E (common-base current gain) and β = I_C/I_B (common-emitter current gain).
Currents: I_E = I_B + I_C.
Divide by I_C: I_E/I_C = I_B/I_C + 1, i.e. 1/α = 1/β + 1.
Hence β = α/(1 − α) and α = β/(1 + β). Since α is slightly less than 1 (e.g. 0.98), β is large (e.g. 49).
An extrinsic semiconductor is a pure semiconductor doped with a small amount of impurity, which greatly increases its conductivity.

N-type: a pentavalent donor introduces an energy level just below the conduction band (≈ 0.01–0.05 eV). At room temperature nearly all donor electrons are excited into the conduction band, so electrons are majority carriers.
P-type: a trivalent acceptor introduces an energy level just above the valence band; valence electrons easily move into it, leaving holes — the majority carriers.

The band gap of the host (Si 1.1 eV) is unchanged, but the small donor/acceptor ionisation energy means many carriers are available, so conductivity σ = e(nμ_e + pμ_h) is much higher than in the intrinsic material and is controlled by the doping level.
